sections.heading: Core idea
paragraphs: Philosophy literally means love of wisdom (from Greek philo, love, and sophia, wisdom). It is a continuing inquiry into fundamental questions about reality, knowledge, truth, value, justice, mind and language.

Philosophy has no single narrow subject matter like many specialized sciences. It investigates broad questions that cross subject boundaries and examines the assumptions behind ordinary beliefs and established claims.

sections.heading: How philosophical inquiry works
bullets: Wonder raises questions about things that may otherwise be taken for granted.
Reason gives arguments for answers rather than relying only on authority or habit.
Analysis clarifies concepts and separates a complex issue into parts.
Comparison considers alternative explanations or positions.
Evaluation tests whether reasons and evidence support a conclusion.
Philosophy is both an activity (questioning, analyzing and arguing) and the ideas produced by that activity.

sections.heading: Constructive and critical sides
paragraphs: The critical side examines, clarifies and evaluates claims and answers. The constructive side develops defensible answers and principles. Criticism is not simply rejection: careful criticism can improve an idea or reveal what evidence is still needed.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Define philosophy etymologically and explain why this phrase alone does not fully describe philosophical practice.
Explain why philosophy is difficult to define by one specific subject matter.
Use an example to show how a philosophical question is analyzed, compared and evaluated.

sections.heading: Having a philosophy and doing philosophy
paragraphs: Having a philosophy is holding a set of beliefs or a personal outlook. Doing philosophy means reflecting critically on beliefs, testing reasons, clarifying meanings and considering alternatives. Having opinions alone is not enough to count as philosophical inquiry.

sections.heading: Common features
bullets: Philosophy seeks rational, critical and coherent understanding.
It examines the world broadly and asks how separate facts fit together.
It is reflective: it looks again at assumptions that common sense may leave unexamined.
It is open to disagreement because people may use different assumptions, experiences or interpretations of incomplete evidence.
It values careful argument, intellectual openness and willingness to revise a position when reasons require it.

sections.heading: Four core fields
bullets: Metaphysics studies reality and existence: what kinds of things exist, and what is ultimately real?
Epistemology studies knowledge: what knowledge is, what its sources and limits are, and how a belief can be justified.
Axiology studies value, including ethics (right and wrong) and aesthetics (beauty and artistic value).
Logic studies correct reasoning and the standards used to distinguish stronger arguments from weaker ones.

sections.heading: Why philosophy matters
paragraphs: Philosophy develops disciplined reasoning, clearer communication, careful judgment and the ability to examine assumptions. These abilities help people assess claims in study, public discussion and everyday decisions. Logic is especially useful as a tool for constructing and evaluating arguments.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Distinguish having a philosophy from doing philosophy.
Match metaphysics, epistemology, axiology and logic to their central questions.
Explain two practical benefits of studying philosophy and connect each to a skill.

sections.heading: What an argument is
paragraphs: An argument is a group of statements in which one or more statements (premises) are offered as reasons for another statement (the conclusion). It makes an inferential claim: the premises are intended to support the conclusion. A statement is a claim that can be true or false; questions and commands are not statements.

sections.heading: Parts and recognition
bullets: Premises provide evidence, reasons or support.
The conclusion is the claim the reasoning aims to establish.
Conclusion cues include therefore, thus, hence and consequently; premise cues include because, since, given that and for. These are clues, not guarantees.
To identify an argument, ask whether a claim is being supported by another claim. Reorder the passage into premise(s) and conclusion if that makes the reasoning clearer.
A passage may contain an unstated premise or conclusion. Make an implicit claim explicit only when it is needed to understand the intended inference.

sections.heading: Arguments versus nonarguments
bullets: A report or explanation may describe why something happened without trying to prove a disputed conclusion.
An illustration gives examples of a claim; an explanation tells how or why something occurred.
A conditional statement (‘if P, then Q’) by itself is not an argument, though it can be used as a premise in one.
A disagreement, question, command or simple list usually has no inference from premises to conclusion.

sections.heading: Worked identification
paragraphs: ‘The road is wet because it rained overnight.’ If this is offered to establish that the road is wet, the conclusion is ‘the road is wet’ and the premise is ‘it rained overnight.’ The word because introduces the reason. Context matters: the same sentence could instead be explaining an already accepted observation.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Underline the conclusion first, then label each supporting premise.
Explain why a statement can be true while the argument containing it is poorly supported.
Distinguish an argument from an explanation, illustration and conditional statement.

sections.heading: Deductive reasoning
paragraphs: A deductive argument claims that its conclusion follows necessarily from its premises. If the premises are true and the reasoning is valid, the conclusion cannot be false. Example: All mammals are warm-blooded; whales are mammals; therefore whales are warm-blooded.

sections.heading: Inductive reasoning
paragraphs: An inductive argument claims that its premises make the conclusion probable, not certain. It often generalizes from observed cases, predicts a future event or infers an explanation from evidence. Example: many sampled buses on this route arrived late, so the next bus is likely to be late.

sections.heading: How to tell them apart
bullets: Look at the inferential claim: does the author present the conclusion as necessary, or as likely/probable?
Deduction is assessed mainly by validity and soundness; induction by strength and cogency.
Words such as probably or likely can signal induction, but wording alone is not decisive. Classify by the support the argument claims to provide.
A generalization from a limited sample is inductive even when expressed confidently.

sections.heading: Evaluating deductive arguments
bullets: Validity concerns form: an argument is valid when it is impossible for all its premises to be true and its conclusion false.
Validity does not mean that the premises are actually true.
Soundness requires both validity and true premises. A sound argument therefore has a true conclusion.
A valid argument can have a false premise; an invalid argument can accidentally have a true conclusion.

sections.heading: Evaluating inductive arguments
bullets: Strength measures how much the premises support the conclusion; a strong argument makes a false conclusion unlikely if its premises are true.
Cogency requires a strong inductive argument with true premises.
Assess sample size and representativeness, relevant background evidence, alternative explanations and the reliability of the observations.
A weak argument may have true premises but still provide little support for its conclusion.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: State whether an argument is deductive or inductive and explain the kind of support it claims.
Separate truth of premises from validity or strength of inference.
Use the definitions to distinguish valid, sound, strong and cogent.

topics.title: Meaning, use and kinds of meaning

sections.heading: Language in reasoning
paragraphs: Logic studies arguments expressed through language, so unclear wording can hide structure or create apparent support. Philosophy of language examines how words and expressions acquire meaning, how meaning is communicated and how language relates to thought and the world.

sections.heading: Cognitive and emotive meaning
bullets: Cognitive meaning conveys information that can be assessed as true or false.
Emotive meaning expresses or evokes feelings and attitudes. Persuasive language can influence an audience even when it contributes no evidence.
A sentence may combine both functions. When evaluating an argument, identify which part states evidence and which part mainly expresses approval, disapproval or emotion.

sections.heading: Intension and extension
bullets: A term’s intension is the set of attributes or meaning associated with it (its connotation).
A term’s extension is the objects or members to which it applies (its denotation).
Terms with different intensions may have the same extension in a particular context; the extension can also change as the world or context changes.
In definition questions, check whether the response explains the term’s attributes, lists its members, or does both.

sections.heading: Ambiguity and precision
paragraphs: A key term should keep a sufficiently clear and consistent meaning throughout an argument. If a word shifts meaning between premises and conclusion, the reasoning may appear stronger than it is. Define important or disputed terms before evaluating the inference.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Give one example of cognitive meaning and one of emotive meaning.
Explain intension and extension using a familiar class such as ‘student’ or ‘river.’
Describe how an ambiguous term can make an argument misleading.

sections.heading: What definitions do
paragraphs: A definition explains the meaning of a word or expression. Definitions can remove vagueness, clarify a debate, explain a new term, influence attitudes, or theoretically characterize a concept. The purpose determines what makes a definition appropriate.

sections.heading: Major types
bullets: A lexical definition reports established ordinary usage; it can be accurate or inaccurate as a report.
A stipulative definition assigns a meaning for a particular discussion or new use; it is not judged true or false in the ordinary way, but should be clear and useful.
A precising definition narrows a vague term for a specific purpose, such as setting an eligibility threshold.
A theoretical definition explains a term within a theory, identifying the role or nature assigned to the thing.
A persuasive definition uses emotionally loaded language to influence attitudes while appearing to define neutrally.

sections.heading: Extensional and intensional techniques
bullets: Denotative (extensional) methods identify members of a class: listing individual examples, naming subclasses, or pointing to representative cases.
Connotative (intensional) methods state the defining attributes. A common method gives the nearest genus (broader class) and the differentia (feature that distinguishes the term within that class).
An ostensive definition identifies something by pointing to an example; it helps with concrete objects but may not capture the full class.
Choose a method that covers the intended cases without including unrelated ones.

sections.heading: Criteria for a good lexical definition
bullets: State essential meaning rather than incidental features.
Avoid circularity: do not define a word using itself or a close synonym that requires the same explanation.
Avoid language that is obscure, ambiguous or needlessly figurative.
Avoid being too broad (including things outside the term) or too narrow (excluding valid instances).
Prefer an affirmative definition when the term names a positive class; negative definitions are useful only when absence is central.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Classify a definition by its purpose before judging it.
Build an intensional definition using genus and differentia.
Diagnose whether a sample definition is circular, too broad, too narrow or unclear, and revise it.

units.title: Chapter 4 - Basic Concepts of Critical Thinking

sections.heading: Critical thinking
paragraphs: Critical thinking is reasonable, reflective and responsible judgment focused on deciding what to believe or do. It combines cognitive skills (analyzing, interpreting, evaluating and inferring) with intellectual dispositions (willingness to seek reasons, examine one’s own beliefs and revise them when warranted). It is not fault-finding or rejecting every claim.

sections.heading: Intellectual standards
bullets: Clarity: is the claim understandable, and can it be illustrated?
Accuracy: is it supported by reliable information?
Precision: are important details sufficiently specific?
Relevance: does the information bear on the question?
Consistency: do claims fit together, or contradict each other?
Logicalness: do the reasons support the conclusion?
Breadth and depth: are alternative viewpoints and important complexities considered?
Fairness: are positions represented impartially, including those one disagrees with?

sections.heading: Good discussion and argument
bullets: State a position clearly and offer relevant reasons or evidence.
Listen to understand the other view before replying; represent it accurately.
Address the strongest relevant objection rather than changing the subject.
Distinguish evidence from assumption, and acknowledge uncertainty or limits.
Revise a conclusion when better reasons or evidence become available.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Define critical thinking and include both thinking skills and intellectual dispositions.
Apply at least four intellectual standards to a short claim.
Explain why criticism does not mean automatic disagreement.

sections.heading: Characteristics of a critical thinker
bullets: Curiosity: asks relevant questions and looks for evidence.
Open-mindedness: considers alternatives without treating every view as equally supported.
Intellectual humility: recognizes limits and possible error.
Intellectual courage: examines ideas that may be uncomfortable or unpopular.
Persistence and discipline: follows an issue through rather than settling for a convenient answer.
Fair-mindedness: applies the same standards to one’s own claims and other people’s claims.

sections.heading: Common barriers
bullets: Egocentrism treats one’s own perspective as the only reasonable one; sociocentrism treats group beliefs as unquestionable.
Wishful thinking favors conclusions because they are comforting or desirable.
Prejudice and stereotyping judge before examining relevant evidence.
Appeal to authority or tradition accepts a claim without checking whether the source or reasons are adequate.
Emotional pressure, haste, overconfidence and selective attention can distort judgment.
A practical response is to pause, identify assumptions, seek counterevidence and use consistent standards.

sections.heading: Benefits and application
paragraphs: Critical thinking supports better problem solving, learning, communication and decision making. In practice: define the question, gather relevant and credible evidence, identify assumptions, compare explanations, evaluate the reasoning, then state a proportionate conclusion and its limits.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Explain a barrier with an example and name a strategy for reducing its effect.
Distinguish open-mindedness from accepting every claim.
Apply the step-by-step critical-thinking process to a real or hypothetical decision.

sections.heading: What makes reasoning fallacious
paragraphs: A fallacy is a defect in reasoning that weakens an argument beyond merely having a false premise. A fallacious pattern can make a conclusion seem supported when the reasons do not adequately establish it. Identify the exact gap rather than relying only on a fallacy label.

sections.heading: Fallacies of relevance
bullets: Appeal to force (ad baculum) uses a threat instead of relevant support.
Appeal to pity (ad misericordiam) asks for sympathy as if it proved the conclusion.
Appeal to the people (ad populum) treats popularity, emotion or group enthusiasm as evidence of truth.
Ad hominem attacks the person advancing a claim instead of addressing the reasons. Criticism of relevant credibility can matter, but personal abuse does not refute an argument.
Straw man distorts or weakens an opponent’s position and attacks the altered version.
Missing the point (ignoratio elenchi) offers reasons that may support a different conclusion from the one at issue.

sections.heading: Exam method
bullets: Write the conclusion and premises in neutral language.
Ask whether each premise is relevant to that conclusion.
Name the fallacy only after explaining how the support fails.
Separate a possibly relevant source-credibility question from an irrelevant personal attack.

sections.heading: Fallacies of weak induction
bullets: Appeal to an unqualified authority relies on a source outside the relevant expertise or treats authority as conclusive.
Appeal to ignorance claims a proposition is true because it has not been disproved, or false because it has not been proved.
Hasty generalization draws a broad conclusion from too few or unrepresentative cases.
False cause assumes a causal connection without adequate evidence; post hoc treats sequence alone (‘after this, therefore because of this’) as proof of cause.
Slippery slope predicts an extreme chain of consequences without showing that the links are likely.

sections.heading: Fallacies of presumption
bullets: Begging the question assumes in the premises what the conclusion is supposed to prove, often in different words.
Complex question bundles an unsupported assumption into a question so that either simple answer appears to accept it.
False dilemma presents too few alternatives as if they were the only possibilities.
Suppressed evidence selectively omits relevant information that could weaken the conclusion.

sections.heading: Ambiguity and grammatical analogy
bullets: Equivocation shifts the meaning of a key word within the argument.
Amphiboly arises from ambiguous sentence structure, allowing more than one reading.
Composition wrongly transfers a property of parts to the whole; division wrongly transfers a property of the whole to each part.
These errors exploit language or part-whole assumptions rather than providing the needed support.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Classify whether the main defect is relevance, weak evidence, an unsupported presumption or ambiguity.
For each example, point to the exact premise or language that causes the error.
Rewrite a fallacious argument into a fair question or a claim supported by adequate evidence.

sections.heading: Standard categorical form
paragraphs: A categorical proposition affirms or denies a relation between two classes. In standard form it contains a quantifier, subject term (S), copula, and predicate term (P). ‘All S are P’ and ‘No S are P’ affirm or deny inclusion or exclusion between classes.

sections.heading: The four standard forms
bullets: A (universal affirmative): All S are P. Example: All roses are flowers.
E (universal negative): No S are P. Example: No squares are circles.
I (particular affirmative): Some S are P. Example: Some students are athletes.
O (particular negative): Some S are not P. Example: Some birds are not flyers.
In categorical logic, ‘some’ means at least one; it does not mean ‘some but not all.’

sections.heading: Quality, quantity and distribution
bullets: Quantity is universal (all/no) or particular (some). Quality is affirmative (A/I) or negative (E/O).
A distributes its subject only: it says something about every S, not every P.
E distributes both terms: it excludes every S from every P.
I distributes neither term: it says at least one member belongs to both classes.
O distributes its predicate only: it identifies at least one S outside P.
Distribution indicates whether a proposition refers to every member of a class; it is central when testing immediate inferences and syllogisms.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Translate a sentence into standard A, E, I or O form.
For each form, identify quantity, quality, subject distribution and predicate distribution.
Do not interpret ‘some’ as ‘some but not all’ unless the wording explicitly says so.

topics.title: Venn diagrams, opposition and immediate inference

sections.heading: Representing propositions with Venn diagrams
bullets: Draw overlapping circles for the subject class S and predicate class P.
For universal claims (A and E), shade the region that must be empty: A shades S outside P; E shades the overlap.
For particular claims (I and O), place an X in a region that must contain at least one member: I in the overlap; O in S outside P.
Shade before placing an X. If an X could belong in either of two unshaded regions and the proposition does not tell which, place it on the boundary between those regions.

sections.heading: Square of opposition
bullets: Contradictories are A–O and E–I: they cannot both be true and cannot both be false.
Contraries are A–E: they cannot both be true, though both can be false.
Subcontraries are I–O: they can both be true, but cannot both be false.

Subalternation traditionally relates A to I and E to O: truth flows from universal to particular and falsity from particular to universal, provided the traditional assumption of existing members is made.

The modern (Boolean) interpretation does not assume that the subject class exists. Therefore the traditional existential subalternation does not automatically hold; distinguish which square the question uses.

sections.heading: Immediate inferences
bullets: Conversion switches subject and predicate. It is valid for E and I; conversion by limitation is traditionally used for A only when existence is assumed; it is not valid for O.
Obversion changes quality and replaces the predicate with its complement. It is valid for all four forms: ‘All S are P’ becomes ‘No S are non-P.’
Contraposition switches subject and predicate and replaces both with their complements. It is valid for A and O; not generally valid for E and I.
Use a Venn diagram or standard form to verify an inference rather than relying on how plausible its wording sounds.

sections.heading: Final exam review
bullets: Identify the proposition form, then mark the diagram and distribution.
For opposition questions, label the relation and state exactly what can or cannot be true together.
For conversion, obversion and contraposition, write each transformation step and check validity for the original form.
Keep the existential assumption explicit whenever a traditional-square inference depends on a class having members.
